pfj-001.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-001.title: Choosing a compiled deployment
pfj-001.instructions: A team builds a C++ application and must distribute it to computers with two different processor architectures. The source code is unchanged. What must the team normally prepare for deployment?
options: A separately compiled executable for each target architecture
One processor-specific executable that is guaranteed to run on both architectures
The source file only; the target computer converts it automatically without a compiler or interpreter
A Java `.class` file for each architecture
hints: Distinguish portable source code from the machine-specific binary produced by compilation.
pfj-001.explanation: The source can be portable, but the compiled binary is produced for a particular target processor. The team therefore needs a suitable build for each architecture.

pfj-002.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-002.title: Interpreted-language deployment trade-off
pfj-002.instructions: A Python program is copied from a developer’s computer to a server. The source file is present, but the program cannot start because the server lacks the required language runtime. Which explanation best fits this situation?
options: The server needs a compatible interpreter to execute the source
The source must first be converted into an Intel-specific executable
Python source code can run only on the processor on which it was written
The JDK is required because Python programs execute as Java bytecode
hints: Think about what performs the translation/execution on the target system.
pfj-002.explanation: In the interpreted-language model from the course, the interpreter is required on each target system. Portable source alone is not enough if the runtime is missing.

pfj-003.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-003.title: Why Java bytecode is portable
pfj-003.instructions: A `.class` file produced on an ARM development computer is moved to an Intel computer. Both computers have a suitable Java platform installed. Why can the same bytecode run on both?
options: The JVM on each computer executes the platform-independent Java bytecode
The `.class` file contains separate Intel and ARM machine-code sections
Java recompiles the original `.java` source on the target, even though only the `.class` file was copied
The processor treats Java bytecode as ordinary native instructions
hints: Identify what the JVM does and what is shared between the two machines.
pfj-003.explanation: Java compilation produces bytecode for the JVM rather than native instructions for one processor. Each system’s JVM provides the processor-specific execution layer.

pfj-004.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-004.title: Selecting the required Java installation
pfj-004.instructions: A developer must write Java code, compile it, debug it and run the resulting program. Which installation is intended to provide the necessary development tools as well as the runtime?
hints: Separate the runtime needed by users from the toolset needed by developers.
pfj-004.explanation: The JDK includes the JRE and development tools such as the compiler and debugger. A JRE is sufficient for running bytecode, but not for the full development workflow.

pfj-005.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-005.title: Java build and run sequence
pfj-005.instructions: You have written `Hello.java` and want to compile and then run it from the command line. Which sequence is correct?
hints: One command compiles source into bytecode; the other starts the JVM for the compiled class.
pfj-005.explanation: `javac` compiles the `.java` source and creates a `.class` file. The `java` command then launches the JVM to execute the class; the class name is used without the extension.

pfj-006.category: The Java Platform and Your First Java Program
pfj-006.title: Resolving a Scanner compilation error
pfj-006.instructions:
A program contains
```java
Scanner keyboard = new Scanner(System.in);
```
but the compiler reports that it cannot find the symbol `Scanner`. The program has no import statements. Which change addresses the likely cause?
options:
Add
```java
import java.util.Scanner;
```
before the class declaration

Add
```java
package Scanner;
```
inside the main method
hints: Consider whether Scanner is automatically available in every source file or belongs to a library package.
pfj-006.explanation: Scanner is in `java.util`, not in the automatically imported `java.lang` package. Importing `java.util.Scanner` makes the class name available to the source file.

pfj-007.category: The Java Platform and Your First Java Program
pfj-007.title: Finding the application entry point
pfj-007.instructions: A Java application contains several classes and many methods. When the application is launched in the basic structure taught in this course, where does execution begin?
options:
In the `main` method with the standard
```java
public static void main(String[] args)
```
entry-point form
In the first constructor declared in the project
In the first method in alphabetical order
In whichever class contains the most attributes
hints: Think about the method the runtime looks for when starting a basic Java application.
pfj-007.explanation:
The course’s first-program structure uses
```java
public static void main(String[] args)
```
as the application entry point. Other methods are called from executing code; their presence alone does not start them.

pfj-008.category: The Java Platform and Your First Java Program
pfj-008.title: Using packages to organise a project
pfj-008.instructions: Two teams both create a class named `Report`, but the classes serve unrelated parts of a larger application. Which design choice best helps organise the code and distinguish the two classes?
options: Place the classes in appropriately named packages
Give both classes the same fully qualified name
Put all source files into one method
hints: Consider how a package relates to a group of source files and to class names.
pfj-008.explanation: Packages group related source files and help prevent naming conflicts. Two classes can share a simple name when their package-qualified names differ.

pfj-009.title: Making an algorithm usable by a simple robot
pfj-009.instructions: You are writing instructions for a robot that must order a pizza. The instruction “choose a suitable pizza” is too vague for the robot to carry out. What is the best next step when refining the algorithm?
options: Replace the vague instruction with explicit steps, inputs, tests and calculations the robot can perform
Leave the instruction as it is because the robot can infer human preferences
Describe only the final pizza and omit the actions required to order it
Convert the instruction directly to a Java class name
hints: Ask whether each step tells the machine exactly what information to use and what action to perform.
pfj-009.explanation: An algorithm must be elaborated to the level understood by the system executing it. A useful refinement specifies concrete actions such as requesting input, presenting choices, testing selections, repeating where needed and computing the amount due.

pfj-010.title: Ordering the steps in a sum algorithm
pfj-010.instructions: A program must ask the user for two numbers and display their sum. Which sequence of algorithmic steps is logically complete?
options: Request the first number; request the second; calculate the sum; display the sum
Calculate the sum; request both numbers; display the sum
Display the sum; request the first number; calculate; request the second number
Request the first number; display it as the sum; request the second number
hints: A calculation cannot use values that have not yet been obtained.
pfj-010.explanation: Both inputs must be available before the addition can be performed. The calculated result is then sent to the output step.

pfj-011.title: Selecting the necessary algorithm actions
pfj-011.instructions: A guessing game repeatedly asks for a number until the guess matches a stored answer. After each guess it reports whether the guess is too low or too high. Which algorithm actions are essential to this task? Select all that apply.
options: Test a condition and choose an appropriate response
Repeat the guessing steps until the stopping condition is met
Compute or compare values to determine the response
Run the same output step exactly once and then stop
hints: Trace one unsuccessful guess and then a successful guess. What must the algorithm do in both cases?
pfj-011.explanation: The algorithm must obtain each guess, compare it with the answer, select the low/high/correct response and repeat until the guess is correct. It therefore uses input, testing, repetition and comparison.

pfj-012.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-012.title: Comparing language implementation trade-offs
pfj-012.instructions: A project prioritises direct execution speed and does not mind producing a different executable for each processor type. Which language-implementation approach best matches those priorities in the course comparison?
options: Compile to processor-specific binary code before execution
Interpret the source text on every run
Run Java bytecode without a JVM
Store the source only and omit all translation
hints: Compare the course’s stated execution-speed and processor-dependency trade-offs.
pfj-012.explanation: The compiled-language model produces binary code that the target processor can execute directly. The course associates this with fast execution, but also with platform-specific binaries and recompilation when code changes.

pfj-013.category: The Java Platform and Your First Java Program
pfj-013.title: Understanding Java platform components
pfj-013.instructions: A student says: “The JDK, JRE and JVM are three names for the same thing.” Which response is the most accurate?
options: They are related but distinct: the JVM executes bytecode, the JRE supplies the runtime and API, and the JDK adds development tools
The JVM is the compiler, the JRE is the IDE, and the JDK is the source file
The JRE contains only an editor; the JDK contains only bytecode
The JDK is needed on every computer that runs a Java application
hints: Think of the execution engine, the runtime package around it, and the extra tools used to develop programs.
pfj-013.explanation: The JVM is the virtual processor for bytecode. The JRE combines the JVM and Java API needed to run programs. The JDK contains the JRE plus tools such as compilation and debugging utilities.

pfj-014.title: Choosing suitable variable types
pfj-014.instructions: A program stores a person’s age in whole years, a measured distance that may contain decimals, and whether a door is locked. Which type choices are most suitable?
options: `int` for age, `double` for distance, `boolean` for the lock state
`double` for age, `boolean` for distance, `char` for the lock state
`boolean` for age, `int` for distance, `double` for the lock state
hints: Match each value to whether it is a whole number, a potentially fractional number or a true/false state.
pfj-014.explanation: Age is naturally represented as an integer count, a measured distance may require a floating-point type, and a lock state has two logical values. `int`, `double` and `boolean` fit those roles.

pfj-015.title: Preventing accidental reassignment of a constant
pfj-015.instructions: A program uses the same VAT percentage in several calculations. The percentage should remain unchanged while the program runs. Which implementation best expresses that requirement?
options: Declare one `final` variable and use it in each calculation
Repeat the numeric literal in every calculation and change it whenever needed
Store it in a variable named `vat` and rely on the programmer not to change it
Declare it as a local variable inside every calculation
hints: Look for the language feature that prevents reassignment after initialization and avoids repeated literal values.
pfj-015.explanation: A `final` variable cannot be reassigned after initialization. Defining the rate once makes the intention explicit and avoids inconsistent copies of the same literal throughout the program.

pfj-016.title: Fixing a narrowing conversion
hints: The conversion goes from a floating-point type to an integer type, so consider an explicit cast.
pfj-016.explanation: Assigning a `double` to an `int` is a narrowing conversion and is not allowed implicitly. `(int) price` makes the conversion explicit; the fractional part is discarded rather than rounded.

pfj-017.title: Predicting integer and floating-point division
hints: Determine the type of the division before considering the type of the variable receiving its result.
pfj-017.explanation: In `a / b`, both operands are integers, so integer division produces `2`; assigning that result to a `double` gives `2.0`. Casting `a` before division makes the operation floating-point and produces `2.5`.

pfj-018.title: Understanding truncation when casting
hints: An explicit cast to an integer does not perform the same operation as rounding to the nearest integer.
pfj-018.explanation: Casting this positive floating-point value to `int` discards the fractional part. It does not round 8.9 up to 9.

pfj-019.title: Using modulo to identify repeating cycles
pfj-019.instructions: A program numbers items from zero and must perform a special action on every fifth item: item 0, 5, 10, 15, and so on. Which condition identifies those item numbers?
hints: The remainder is zero exactly when the number is divisible by five.
pfj-019.explanation: The modulo operator returns the remainder after division. A remainder of zero identifies multiples of five, including zero.

pfj-020.title: Tracing pre-increment and post-increment
hints: Trace each statement separately: post-increment uses the old value first; pre-increment changes the value before it is used.
pfj-020.explanation: Initially `i` is 4. `i++` assigns 4 to `first` and then changes `i` to 5. `++i` changes `i` to 6 before assigning it to `second`.

pfj-021.title: Combining arithmetic and assignment
hints: Rewrite each compound assignment as an ordinary calculation followed by assignment, then evaluate in order.
pfj-021.explanation: `total += step` gives 17. `step *= 2` gives 10. Finally, `total %= step` means `total = 17 % 10`, leaving 7.

pfj-022.title: Building a valid range condition
pfj-022.instructions: A program classifies people aged from 18 through 67 inclusive as being in the active age range. Which condition correctly includes both boundary values and excludes values outside the range?
hints: Both limits must be satisfied, and “through” means the endpoints are included.
pfj-022.explanation: The `&&` operator requires both comparisons to be true. Using `>=` and `<=` includes ages 18 and 67.

pfj-023.title: Using OR to detect invalid values
pfj-023.instructions: A valid score must be between 0 and 100 inclusive. Which condition detects a score that is outside this range?
hints: An invalid value is either below the minimum or above the maximum; it cannot be both at once.
pfj-023.explanation: A value is outside the allowed range when at least one boundary is violated. `||` correctly detects either case; `&&` would require an impossible value to be below zero and above 100 at the same time.

pfj-024.title: Negating a logical condition
pfj-024.instructions: A boolean variable `available` is true when a seat can be booked. Which expression is true exactly when the seat is not available?
hints: Use the unary logical operator that reverses a boolean value.
pfj-024.explanation: `!` negates its operand: true becomes false and false becomes true. Therefore `!available` represents the unavailable state.

pfj-025.title: Applying operator precedence
pfj-025.instructions:
What value is assigned to `result`?
```java
int result = 2 + 3 * 4;
```
hints: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition.
pfj-025.explanation: The multiplication is evaluated first: 3 × 4 = 12. Then 2 is added, so the result is 14. Parentheses would make a different intended grouping explicit.

pfj-026.title: Making an expression unambiguous
pfj-026.instructions: A shop calculates a discount on the combined prices of two items. Which expression clearly applies the discount rate to the sum of both prices?
hints: The subtotal must be calculated before the rate is applied.
pfj-026.explanation: Parentheses group the two prices into one subtotal, and multiplication then applies the discount rate to that subtotal. Without the parentheses, multiplication binds more tightly than addition.

pfj-027.title: Choosing between AND and OR
pfj-027.instructions: A user may enter a command only if they are an administrator and the account is active. Which condition represents that rule?
hints: The rule requires both independent requirements to hold.
pfj-027.explanation: Both administrator status and active-account status are mandatory, so the conditions must be joined with logical AND (`&&`). OR would allow either one alone to grant access.

pfj-028.title: Using a compound assignment correctly
pfj-028.instructions: A running total is stored in `sum`. A newly read value is stored in `next`. Which statement adds `next` to the existing total without replacing the total with `next`?
hints: The operation must both calculate the sum and store it back in the original variable.
pfj-028.explanation: `sum += next` is equivalent to `sum = sum + next`. A plain assignment would discard the previous total; `==` compares values rather than updating one.

pfj-029.title: Choosing a character representation
pfj-029.instructions: A program must store one individual character, such as the grade letter `B`, rather than an arbitrary-length name. Which declaration is most appropriate?
hints: A single character literal uses a different form from a text String.
pfj-029.explanation: A `char` stores one character and uses single quotes around the character literal. A String represents text and uses double quotes.

pfj-030.title: Producing a quoted word in output
pfj-030.instructions: A program must print exactly `Welcome to "Java"` on one line. Which statement correctly writes the quotation marks as part of the output?
hints: The double quotes that delimit a String literal must be distinguished from quotes that should appear in the output.
pfj-030.explanation: The inner quotation marks must be escaped as `\"` so they are treated as characters in the String rather than as the end of the literal.

pfj-031.title: Selecting a conditional expression
pfj-031.instructions: A variable `status` should receive the String `"adult"` when `age >= 18`, and `"minor"` otherwise. Which assignment expresses this compact two-way choice?
hints: A conditional expression has a condition followed by the true value and the false value, separated by `?` and `:`.
pfj-031.explanation: The ternary operator evaluates the boolean condition and yields one of the two String values. Its result can be assigned directly to `status`.

pfj-032.title: Choosing integer or floating-point arithmetic
pfj-032.instructions: A program calculates an average from two integer test scores and must preserve fractional results. Which expression ensures the division is performed using floating-point arithmetic?
hints: At least one operand in the division must be floating point before the division takes place.
pfj-032.explanation: Casting the sum to `double` before dividing makes the division floating-point. Dividing two integers first would discard any fractional part, even if the result were later assigned to a double.

pfj-033.title: Replacing repeated literal values with a named constant
pfj-033.instructions: Several methods compare a temperature against the same maximum allowed value. Later, the value may need to change. Which design is most maintainable?
options: Declare one clearly named `final` constant and use it in every comparison
Copy the numeric value into each comparison so each method is independent
Use a new randomly generated limit in each method
Declare a local variable with a different value in each method
hints: Look for a single source of truth that cannot accidentally be changed at runtime.
pfj-033.explanation: A shared `final` constant avoids duplicated “magic numbers” and keeps all comparisons consistent when the allowed limit changes.

pfj-034.title: Choosing a branch structure for a grade calculation
pfj-034.instructions: A program assigns A for scores of at least 90, B for 80–89, C for 70–79, D for 60–69 and E below 60. Which ordering makes an `if / else if` chain work correctly?
options: Test thresholds from highest to lowest: 90, 80, 70, 60, then else
Test thresholds from lowest to highest: 60, 70, 80, 90, then else
Use four independent `if` statements and allow every matching branch to run
Test only whether the score is greater than zero
hints: An `else if` chain executes the first matching branch, so consider what happens to a score of 95 if the lowest threshold is tested first.
pfj-034.explanation: Testing from the highest threshold down ensures that a score such as 95 matches A immediately. If 60 were tested first, every higher score would be classified as E before later tests could run.

pfj-035.title: Checking inclusive grade boundaries
pfj-035.instructions: Using the grade rules A: 90 and above, B: 80–89, C: 70–79, D: 60–69, E: below 60, what grade should a score of exactly 80 receive?
hints: Check the lower boundary of each band; the band beginning at 80 includes 80.
pfj-035.explanation: A score of 80 is below 90 but is at least 80, so it belongs to the B range.

pfj-036.title: Identifying a fall-through bug in switch
hints: In a traditional switch, follow execution after the first matching label until a `break` is reached.
pfj-036.explanation: Case 1 matches and prints A. Because there is no `break` after that statement, execution continues into case 2, prints B, and then stops at its `break`.

pfj-037.title: Using switch for grouped choices
pfj-037.instructions: A program maps the month names `march`, `april` and `may` to the same result, `spring`. In a traditional switch, how can the cases share one output block without repeating the output statement?
options: Let the case labels fall through to one shared statement, then use `break`
Place a `return` after every case label before the output
Use a separate switch statement for each month
Omit the case labels and rely on the default branch
hints: Multiple labels can lead to the same sequence of statements when no statement separates them.
pfj-037.explanation: Adjacent case labels can share one block. Execution enters at the matched label and continues to the common output until `break` exits the switch.

pfj-038.title: Handling an unexpected switch value
pfj-038.instructions: A menu program supports options 1, 2 and 3. The user may enter any integer. What should happen when the input does not match one of the supported options?
options: A `default` branch should handle the unsupported value
The program should silently execute case 1
The switch should repeat every case in order
The compiler should choose the closest numeric case
hints: Consider how the program can provide a defined response when no case matches.
pfj-038.explanation: A `default` branch provides the fallback behavior for values not matched by a listed case, such as displaying an invalid-option message.

pfj-039.title: Understanding a switch expression
options: Because the expression must produce a value for every possible input
Because every switch statement must contain exactly one default branch
Because switch expressions cannot contain String labels
Because Java automatically assigns null to an uncovered case
hints: The result is assigned to a variable, so consider what happens when the input does not match any listed alternative.
pfj-039.explanation: A switch expression must yield a value. If not every possible input is covered by its cases, a default branch is needed to supply the missing result.

pfj-040.title: Returning a value from a switch block
pfj-040.instructions: In a switch expression, one case contains several statements inside `{ ... }` and must produce the String `"invalid"` as the expression result. Which construct supplies that value?
hints: A multi-statement case block in a switch expression needs an explicit value-producing statement.
pfj-040.explanation: `yield` supplies the value returned by that case block to the switch expression. Printing text is a side effect and does not provide the expression’s result.

pfj-041.title: Choosing while for an unknown number of attempts
pfj-041.instructions: A program keeps asking a user to enter a password until the correct password is supplied. The number of attempts is unknown in advance. Which loop is a natural fit?
options: A `while` loop whose condition represents whether the password is still incorrect
A `for` loop that always runs exactly ten times
A sequence of ten separate `if` statements
hints: Choose a loop whose continuation can be based on a condition rather than a predetermined count.
pfj-041.explanation: A `while` loop repeats while its condition is true. The number of attempts is data-dependent, so a condition-controlled loop fits the task.

pfj-042.title: Diagnosing an infinite while loop
options: The loop body never changes `counter`, so the condition remains true
The condition is checked after every statement in the program
`println` automatically resets the counter to zero
hints: Trace the variable used by the condition and check whether the loop body changes it.
pfj-042.explanation: `counter` starts at 0 and is never modified inside the loop. Therefore `counter < 5` remains true forever. A terminating loop needs progress toward a state where its condition becomes false.

pfj-043.title: Choosing do-while for a menu
pfj-043.instructions: A program must display a menu at least once, then ask whether the user wants to see it again. Which loop structure directly supports the requirement that the body runs before the condition is checked?
options: A `for` loop with an initially false condition
hints: Compare whether the condition is checked before or after the first execution of the body.
pfj-043.explanation: A `do ... while` loop executes its body first and tests its condition afterward, so the menu is shown at least once.

pfj-044.title: Counting an inclusive range with for
pfj-044.instructions: Which loop prints every integer from 1 through 5, including both endpoints?
hints: The upper-bound comparison must still be true when the counter is exactly 5.
pfj-044.explanation: Starting at 1 and using `i <= 5` includes 5. Using `< 5` would stop before printing the upper endpoint.

pfj-045.title: Tracing a for loop
hints: Start with the initialization, check the condition before each iteration, then apply the modification after the body.
pfj-045.explanation: The counter starts at 2 and increases by 2 after each print. The values 2, 4, 6 and 8 satisfy `i <= 8`; after 8 the counter becomes 10 and the loop ends.

pfj-046.title: Translating a for loop into while
hints: Preserve the for loop’s order: initialize once, check before the body, then increment after the body.
pfj-046.explanation: The equivalent while loop places initialization before the loop and moves the modification to the end of the body. This preserves the first printed value (0) and the same stopping condition.

pfj-047.title: Distinguishing break from continue
hints: `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration; `break` exits the loop entirely.
pfj-047.explanation: At i=1 and i=2 the values are printed. At i=3, `continue` skips the print. At i=4 it prints 4. At i=5, `break` exits before printing, giving `124`.

pfj-048.title: Understanding variable scope in nested blocks
options: Both print statements compile; `bonus` is available only inside the `if` block
The second print statement can use both `total` and `bonus`
The first print statement cannot use `total` because it was declared outside the block
The declaration of `bonus` changes the value of `total`
hints: A variable declared in an outer block can be used in a nested block; a variable declared in the nested block does not escape it.
pfj-048.explanation: `total` is declared in the method block and is visible inside and after the `if`. `bonus` is local to the `if` block, so it can be used in the first print but not outside that block.

pfj-049.title: Fixing a scope error
pfj-049.instructions:
A method declares
```java
int result = 0;
```
inside an `if` block but tries to return `result` after the closing brace of that block. What is the simplest structural fix?
options: Declare `result` in an enclosing block before the `if`, then assign it inside the `if`
Move the `return` statement to a different class without changing the variable
Declare `result` again after the `if` and expect the inner value to carry over
Change the variable type from `int` to `double`
hints: The variable must be declared in a scope that includes both the assignment and the return statement.
pfj-049.explanation: The return statement cannot see a variable declared only inside the `if` block. Declaring it in the enclosing method block makes it visible both inside the conditional and at the return point.

pfj-050.title: Using separate blocks for separate local variables
pfj-050.instructions: A method contains two separate `if` blocks. Each block declares a local variable named `message`, and neither block uses the other block’s variable. Why can these declarations coexist?
options: Each variable belongs to a different block scope
Java allows duplicate local variables anywhere in one method
The second declaration automatically overwrites the first variable
Local variables are shared across all methods
hints: Compare the visibility regions created by the two pairs of curly braces.
pfj-050.explanation: The first `message` exists only in its declaring block, and the second exists only in the other block. Their scopes do not overlap, so the names do not conflict.

pfj-051.title: Refactoring duplicated steps into a function
pfj-051.instructions: A program asks for three amounts using nearly identical input code. The same input procedure may be needed elsewhere. Which change best improves reuse and reduces duplication?
options: Move the input procedure into a method and call that method each time an amount is needed
Copy the input statements into more places so every calculation is independent
Place all input statements in a comment
Replace the input procedure with a class name
hints: Look for a named block of code that can be called repeatedly from different locations.
pfj-051.explanation: A method packages a reusable algorithm. Calling it for each amount avoids repeating the same implementation and makes the main workflow shorter and easier to read.

pfj-052.title: Returning an average from a method
pfj-052.instructions: A method receives three `double` values and calculates their average. The caller must store that average in a variable. Which method design fits the task?
options: A method with return type `double` that returns the calculated average
A method with return type `void` that only prints the average
A method with no parameters that always returns 0
A method with return type `String` that changes the caller’s variables
hints: The caller needs a value it can assign and use in later calculations.
pfj-052.explanation: The method should return a `double`, because the average is a numeric result that the caller must receive. A `void` method performs an action but does not produce a value for assignment.

pfj-053.title: Choosing a void method
pfj-053.instructions: A method’s only responsibility is to display a formatted report. The caller does not need a result for further calculations. Which return type is appropriate?
hints: Choose a return type based on whether the method must give a value back to its caller.
pfj-053.explanation: The method only performs output and has no result to return. `void` expresses that contract; the other types would require a value of the corresponding type.

pfj-054.title: Using a returned method value in an expression
pfj-054.instructions: A method `average(a, b, c)` returns a `double`. Which call can use its return value directly in a larger expression?
options:
```java
double doubled = printAverage(a, b, c) * 2;
```
where `printAverage` returns void
hints: A non-void method call evaluates to a value that can participate in another expression.
pfj-054.explanation: A method returning `double` produces a value, so the result can be multiplied and assigned. A void method call has no result and cannot be used in an arithmetic expression.

pfj-055.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-055.title: Distinguishing a class from an object
pfj-055.instructions: A program models cars. It defines common fields such as colour, speed and direction, and methods such as start and brake. A particular red car with its own speed is created from that definition. Which statement is correct?
options: The car definition is the class; the particular red car is an object
The particular red car is the class; the definition is an object
The fields are objects and the methods are classes
The class and the particular car are the same thing
hints: Separate the general description shared by a type from one individual instance with its own state.
pfj-055.explanation: The class is the blueprint that describes the shared structure and behavior. Each particular car created from it is a distinct object with its own attribute values.

pfj-056.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-056.title: Choosing attributes and methods for an object
pfj-056.instructions: You are designing a `Ship` class. Which design best separates information describing a ship from actions the ship can perform?
options: Attributes such as capacity and length; methods such as dock and lowerAnchor
Methods such as capacity and length; attributes such as dock and lowerAnchor
Only attributes, because objects do not have behavior
Only methods, because object state is stored in the class name
hints: Classify each item as information about the current state or an action the object can perform.
pfj-056.explanation: Capacity and length describe state and belong in attributes. Docking and lowering an anchor describe behavior and belong in methods.

pfj-057.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-057.title: Creating distinct object instances
options: They refer to two separately created Random objects configured with the same seed
They refer to one shared object because the constructor arguments match
The second declaration copies the first object automatically
hints: Each execution of `new` creates an object; a seed controls the generated sequence, not object identity.
pfj-057.explanation: Each `new Random(10)` call creates a distinct object. Because the seeds are equal, each instance produces the same pseudo-random sequence, but the references point to separate objects.

pfj-058.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-058.title: Generating a fair six-sided die roll
pfj-058.instructions: A `Random` object named `generator` is already available. Which expression produces an integer die result from 1 through 6 inclusive?
hints: The one-argument `nextInt` starts at zero and excludes its bound; shift the range if the die starts at one.
pfj-058.explanation: `nextInt(6)` yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5. Adding one shifts the possible outcomes to 1 through 6.

pfj-059.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-059.title: Generating an inclusive two-digit range
pfj-059.instructions: A lottery program needs a random integer from 50 through 99 inclusive. Which expression produces exactly that range using the two-argument method?
hints: The origin is included and the upper bound is excluded.
pfj-059.explanation: `nextInt(50, 100)` can return 50 up to 99. The second argument is exclusive, so using 99 would omit 99.

pfj-060.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-060.title: Using a seed for repeatable tests
pfj-060.instructions: A developer wants a lottery simulation to generate the same sequence of pseudo-random values every time during debugging. Which approach best supports repeatable tests?
options: Create the Random object with a fixed seed and reuse the same sequence
Create a new unseeded Random object before every generated value
Set the seed to a different value for each test run
hints: A seeded pseudo-random generator reproduces its sequence when initialized with the same seed.
pfj-060.explanation: The same seed produces the same pseudo-random sequence. Fixing the seed makes test runs repeatable, which helps locate and reproduce errors.

pfj-061.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-061.title: Understanding shared object references
options: A new Player object is created when `p1` changes
hints: The second assignment copies a reference, not a separate copy of the object.
pfj-061.explanation: `p1` and `p2` refer to the same Player object. Updating its state through `p1` is therefore visible when the object is accessed through `p2`.

pfj-062.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-062.title: Contrasting primitive and reference assignment
options: 7, because the primitive value was copied when `b` was assigned
8, because primitive variables always remain linked
The code does not compile because primitives cannot be assigned
hints: Primitive assignment copies the current value rather than creating an alias to the original variable.
pfj-062.explanation: `b = a` copies the value 7 into `b`. Incrementing `a` later changes only `a`, so `b` remains 7. This differs from assigning one object reference to another.

pfj-063.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-063.title: Recognising when an object becomes eligible for collection
pfj-063.instructions: A method creates a `Random` object and stores its reference in a local variable. The method ends, and no other variable refers to that object. What is the consequence?
options: The object becomes eligible for garbage collection, which Java performs automatically at a later time
The object is deleted immediately as the method returns
The object is copied into every remaining variable
The program must call `delete` on the object
hints: Consider whether any reference remains and whether garbage collection is immediate or automatic.
pfj-063.explanation: When no references remain, the object is eligible for garbage collection. Java manages this automatically; the course notes that collection is not immediate.

pfj-064.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-064.title: Selecting an import strategy
pfj-064.instructions: A class in one package needs to use a library class named `Random` from `java.util`. Which option allows the source to refer to it by the simple name `Random`?
options:
Add
```java
import java.util.Random;
```
and then use `Random`
Use `Random` without importing it and without a package qualification
Put the import statement inside the constructor body
hints: An import makes a class name available without writing its fully qualified package name each time.
pfj-064.explanation: The explicit import identifies `java.util.Random`, after which the simple class name can be used. Without an import, the fully qualified name must be written.

pfj-065.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-065.title: Understanding String immutability
hints: A String method that appears to modify text may instead return a different String object.
pfj-065.explanation: String objects are immutable. `concat` returns a new String, but the code does not store that returned value. The variable `word` still refers to the original `"cat"`.

pfj-066.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-066.title: Keeping the result of a String operation
pfj-066.instructions:
Suppose `word` is initialized as follows:
```java
String word = "cat";
```
The program wants to keep `word` unchanged and also store the result of adding `"fish"`. Which statement creates the new result?
hints: Since Strings cannot be changed in place, the method’s returned String must be stored if it is needed.
pfj-066.explanation: `concat` returns a new String. Assigning the result to `combined` preserves the original `word` reference and stores the combined text separately.

pfj-067.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-067.title: Comparing String contents rather than references
pfj-067.instructions: Two String variables may refer to different String objects but contain the same characters. Which method should be used to test whether their text is equal?
hints: Separate object identity from equality of the character contents.
pfj-067.explanation: `equals()` compares String contents. `==` compares whether the two references identify the same object, which is not the intended test when comparing text.

pfj-068.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-068.title: Predicting String reference comparisons
options: `a.equals(c)` is true even though `a == c` is false
`a.equals(c)` is false because `c` was created with `new`
`a == c` must be true because the contents match
All three variables must refer to separate objects
hints: Use `equals` for the text and `==` for reference identity.
pfj-068.explanation: The explicit `new String` creates a distinct object, so `a == c` is false. Their characters are the same, so `a.equals(c)` is true.

pfj-069.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-069.title: Choosing next or nextLine for user input
pfj-069.instructions: A user enters the full name `Ada Lovelace`. The program must store the entire name, including the space. Which Scanner call is suitable?
hints: One method reads only up to the next whitespace; the other reads the remainder of the line.
pfj-069.explanation: `nextLine()` reads the complete line, including spaces, up to the newline. `next()` would stop after `Ada` because it ends at whitespace.

pfj-070.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-070.title: Fixing the Scanner nextInt-nextLine issue
options: Call `keyboard.nextLine()` once after `nextInt()` to consume the leftover line break
Create a new String object before calling `nextLine()`
hints: The Enter key leaves a line terminator in the input buffer after the integer has been read.
pfj-070.explanation: `nextInt()` reads the number but leaves the line terminator behind. The immediate `nextLine()` consumes that leftover line break and returns an empty String. An extra `nextLine()` clears it before reading the name.

pfj-071.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-071.title: Choosing StringBuilder for repeated modifications
pfj-071.instructions: A program builds a long message by appending hundreds of pieces of text inside a loop. Which class is the better fit for this pattern, and why?
options: `StringBuilder`, because it can modify its contents without creating a new String for every append
`String`, because its contents can be changed in place
`Scanner`, because it combines input fragments automatically
hints: Consider which of the two text classes is mutable and is designed for repeated changes.
pfj-071.explanation: `StringBuilder` is mutable. Appending text changes the builder rather than creating a new String object on every operation, making it more suitable for frequent modifications.

pfj-072.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-072.title: Tracing chained StringBuilder calls
hints: Each append adds its argument to the current end of the same builder; the calls can be chained.
pfj-072.explanation: The first append changes the builder to `AB`; the second changes it to `ABC`. Printing the builder displays its current content.

pfj-073.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-073.title: Predicting StringBuilder reverse
hints: The method reverses the order of the characters in the builder.
pfj-073.explanation: `reverse()` reverses the content in place. The characters in `drawer` read backward as `reward`.

pfj-074.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-074.title: Understanding left-to-right String concatenation
pfj-074.instructions:
What is printed by this statement?
```java
System.out.println(3 + 7 + " items " + 3 + 7);
```
hints: Before a String is reached, `+` performs numeric addition; after a String is involved, it concatenates from left to right.
pfj-074.explanation: The first two operands are integers, so `3 + 7` becomes 10. Once the String is encountered, later `+` operations concatenate text, giving `10 items 37`.

pfj-075.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-075.title: Building formatted text versus printing it
pfj-075.instructions: A method must return a formatted invoice line as a String so another method can store or process it later. Which call is appropriate?
hints: Distinguish methods that display output from the method that returns a String value.
pfj-075.explanation: `String.format` creates and returns a formatted String object. `printf` and `format` on `System.out` write formatted output to the console.

pfj-076.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-076.title: Formatting a monetary value
pfj-076.instructions: An invoice must display a decimal amount with exactly two digits after the decimal point. Which format specifier is intended for this requirement?
hints: Choose the floating-point specifier and set the requested number of decimal places.
pfj-076.explanation: `%f` formats a floating-point number. The `.2` precision requests two digits after the decimal point; the formatter rounds to that precision.

pfj-077.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-077.title: Aligning formatted output
pfj-077.instructions: A report lists city names in a column of at least 12 character positions, with the text aligned to the left. Which specifier matches that requirement?
hints: For a String, the width sets a minimum field size and the minus sign requests left alignment.
pfj-077.explanation: `%s` is the String conversion, `12` sets a minimum width of 12 positions, and `-` left-aligns the value within that field.

pfj-078.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-078.title: Designing a Rectangle class
pfj-078.instructions: A `Rectangle` object must remember its position and dimensions, and calculate its area and perimeter. Which class design best matches that responsibility?
options: Store x, y, height and width as attributes; provide methods to calculate area and perimeter
Store area and perimeter as method names only; keep no dimensions
Store every Rectangle object inside the class name
Put the position and dimensions only in the `main` method
hints: Separate the state each rectangle must retain from the calculations it can perform using that state.
pfj-078.explanation: Position and dimensions describe each rectangle’s state and belong in instance attributes. Area and perimeter are behaviors/calculations based on those attributes and belong in methods.

pfj-079.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-079.title: Protecting object state from direct changes
pfj-079.instructions: A `Rectangle` class must prevent client code from assigning a negative width directly. Which design provides the appropriate control?
options: Keep width private and expose a public setter that checks the proposed value
Make width public and document that negative values are discouraged
Remove the width attribute and use a package name instead
Make every method private so the client can change width directly
hints: Consider where validation can be enforced so every change to the attribute passes through the same rule.
pfj-079.explanation: A private attribute prevents client code from modifying the field directly. A public setter can validate the proposed width and update the field only when it satisfies the class invariant.

pfj-080.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-080.title: Understanding private attribute access
pfj-080.instructions:
A field
```java
private int speed;
```
is declared in class `Car`. A separate application class creates a Car object and tries to read `myCar.speed`. What should happen?
options: The access is rejected because private fields can be accessed only within their declaring class
The access succeeds because the object was created by the application
The access succeeds whenever both classes have a main method
The access is allowed only if speed is initialized to zero
hints: Access is determined by the declared accessibility modifier, not by which class creates the object.
pfj-080.explanation: A private field is accessible inside its own class only. Client code must use a public method such as a getter when the class chooses to expose that information.

pfj-081.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-081.title: Distinguishing field defaults from local variables
pfj-081.instructions:
A class declares
```java
private int count;
```
and a method declares
```java
int result;
```
without assigning either variable. Which statement is correct?
options: The attribute `count` defaults to 0, but the local variable `result` must be assigned before use
The attribute defaults to null, while the local variable defaults to 0
Neither variable can be used because neither was explicitly initialized
hints: Compare instance attributes with local variables declared inside a method.
pfj-081.explanation: Instance attributes receive default values based on their types; an integral attribute defaults to 0. Local variables are not automatically initialized, so the method must assign `result` before using it.

pfj-082.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-082.title: Avoiding a null reference failure
pfj-082.instructions:
A field is declared as
```java
private String name;
```
and is never assigned a String object. The constructor then calls `name.length()`. What is the likely runtime result?
options: A `NullPointerException`, because the reference field defaults to null
The result is 0 because all object fields default to an empty object
The compiler creates an empty String automatically
The call returns -1 to indicate missing text
hints: An object reference field has a default value; consider whether that value supports method calls.
pfj-082.explanation: Object-reference attributes default to `null`, not to an empty String. Calling an instance method through a null reference causes a `NullPointerException`.

pfj-083.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-083.title: Using this to access a shadowed attribute
options: The parameter name hides the attribute name, so the assignment assigns the parameter to itself
The method needs to return an int before it can update a field
Java does not allow a parameter to have the same name as an attribute
The assignment operator cannot be used inside a method
hints: When a parameter and an attribute share a name, use the `this` reference to identify the current object’s field.
pfj-083.explanation: Inside the method, the unqualified name `width` refers to the parameter. `width = width` therefore changes nothing. The intended assignment is `this.width = width`.

pfj-084.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-084.title: Correcting a setter with a shadowed parameter
pfj-084.instructions: Which implementation correctly stores the new x-coordinate in the current Rectangle object?
hints: The parameter provides the new value; the object’s field is the destination.
pfj-084.explanation: `this.x` identifies the current object’s attribute, while the unqualified `x` on the right refers to the parameter. The assignment copies the supplied value into the field.

pfj-085.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-085.title: Validating values in a setter
pfj-085.instructions: A Car accepts speeds from -20 to 300 inclusive. Its current speed is 50. The setter checks the proposed value and updates the field only when it falls in that interval. What should happen after `setSpeed(500)`?
options: The speed remains 50 and the invalid input can be reported
The speed becomes 500 because setters must always assign their parameter
hints: Check whether 500 satisfies both the minimum and maximum constraints.
pfj-085.explanation: 500 is above the allowed maximum, so the validating setter rejects it and leaves the existing valid state unchanged. This is the purpose of validating the parameter before assigning it.

pfj-086.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-086.title: Choosing which attributes should have setters
pfj-086.instructions: A class stores a calculated identifier that must never change after the object is created. The application may need to display the identifier. Which public interface is the safer design?
options: Provide a getter but no setter for the identifier
Provide a setter that accepts any new identifier
Make the identifier public so all code can update it
Return the identifier only from the constructor and then delete the field
hints: Encapsulation does not require every attribute to be freely changeable; expose only the operations the object should support.
pfj-086.explanation: A getter can expose the identifier without allowing clients to modify it. Omitting a setter helps preserve the object’s invariant after construction.

pfj-087.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-087.title: Using a method return value correctly
pfj-087.instructions: A method `getWidth()` returns an `int`, while `setWidth(int width)` returns `void`. Which statement is valid?
hints: A getter produces a value; a void setter performs an action without returning one.
pfj-087.explanation: `getWidth()` returns an integer that can be assigned to `current`. A void method has no result to assign or print, and the result of a getter call is not an assignable field.

pfj-088.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-088.title: Identifying a valid overloaded method
pfj-088.instructions: A class has `report()` and the programmer wants a second version that reports speed in a caller-supplied unit. Which declaration is a valid overload?
options:
```java
public int report()
```
with no parameters

```java
private void report()
```
with no parameters and the same signature

```java
public void report(String unit, int speed)
```
replacing the original method
hints: Overloading requires the same method name but a different parameter list; changing only the return type is insufficient.
pfj-088.explanation: `report(String unit)` has the same name and a different parameter list, so calls can be resolved by their arguments. A method cannot be overloaded by return type alone.

pfj-089.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-089.title: Understanding constructor availability
pfj-089.instructions: A class `Point` initially declares no constructors. A programmer later adds only `Point(double x, double y)`. Which statement about `new Point()` is correct?
options: It no longer compiles unless a no-argument constructor is explicitly added
It still compiles because Java always adds a no-argument constructor
It calls the two-argument constructor with zero values
It creates a null Point reference
hints: The compiler supplies a no-argument default constructor only when the class declares no constructor at all.
pfj-089.explanation: Once a constructor is declared, Java no longer generates the automatic no-argument default constructor. The class must explicitly declare `Point()` if clients should still be able to call `new Point()`.

pfj-090.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-090.title: Choosing constructor responsibilities
pfj-090.instructions: A `Point` object must be created with initial x and y coordinates. Which design best ensures those values are established as part of object creation?
options: Provide a constructor with x and y parameters and assign them to the object’s attributes
Require every client to create an empty Point and directly modify public fields
Use a getter to assign the coordinates
Put the coordinates in the class name
hints: A constructor runs when a new instance is created and is intended to initialize its state.
pfj-090.explanation: A parameterized constructor receives the initial coordinate values and stores them in the new object. This ensures the object is initialized at creation rather than relying on unrestricted client-side changes.

pfj-091.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-091.title: Preventing invalid state during construction
pfj-091.instructions: A Car constructor currently assigns its speed parameter directly, so `new Car(-1000)` creates an invalid object. The class already has a setter that checks the allowed speed range. What is the best change?
options: Have the constructor call the validating setter with the supplied speed
Remove the validation from the setter
hints: The constructor must enforce the same state rules as later updates.
pfj-091.explanation: Calling the validating setter from the constructor applies the same rule at initialization time. Otherwise, invalid data can enter through construction even though later setter calls are checked.

pfj-092.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-092.title: Reusing constructor initialization logic
pfj-092.instructions: A class has a constructor `Circle(double radius)` that performs validation. The no-argument constructor should create a circle with radius 1.0 while reusing that validation. Which implementation is appropriate?
hints: A constructor can delegate to another constructor in the same class using `this(arguments)`; the call must be first.
pfj-092.explanation: `this(1.0)` invokes the parameterized constructor and reuses its validation. A constructor delegation call must be the first statement in the constructor body.

pfj-093.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-093.title: Recognising constructor delegation order
options: A call to another constructor using `this(...)` must be the first statement
A constructor cannot contain a print statement
A constructor cannot call another constructor
The delegated constructor must have no parameters
hints: Recall the placement rule for constructor chaining.
pfj-093.explanation: Constructor chaining with `this(...)` must appear first so that the target constructor performs initialization before any other statements in the delegating constructor.

pfj-094.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-094.title: Using a copy constructor to create a separate object
pfj-094.instructions: A new Rectangle must start with the same x, y, height and width values as an existing Rectangle, but must be a separate object so later changes do not affect the original. Which approach matches that requirement?
options: Create a new Rectangle through a constructor that accepts the original Rectangle and copies its attribute values
Assign the original reference to a second variable
Return the original Rectangle without creating anything
Set every attribute to its default value
hints: The requirement is for equal initial state but distinct object identity.
pfj-094.explanation: A copy constructor can read the original object’s attributes and initialize a newly allocated Rectangle with those values. Merely assigning the original reference would make both variables point to the same object.

pfj-095.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-095.title: Understanding the default toString result
pfj-095.instructions:
A class has no custom `toString()` method. A program executes this statement:
```java
System.out.println(myObject);
```
What kind of output should the programmer expect from the inherited default implementation?
options: A class-name and hash-code style representation, not a useful description of the object’s fields
All private attribute values formatted automatically
The result of the object’s constructor source code
The name of the variable used to refer to the object
hints: Consider what the inherited Object implementation provides when a class does not override the method.
pfj-095.explanation: The default `toString()` representation is based on the class name and hash code and is generally not meaningful to users. A class should override it when a readable description is required.

pfj-096.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-096.title: Predicting output after overriding toString
hints: When an object is passed to println, its String representation is obtained through toString.
pfj-096.explanation: The overridden method returns `Answer: 42`. `println` invokes `toString()` for the object, so printing the object displays that returned String.

pfj-097.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-097.title: Choosing Math methods for a calculation
pfj-097.instructions: A program needs the positive magnitude of a possibly negative number, the square root of a value, and one number raised to a power. Which set of calls uses the appropriate Math methods?
hints: Match each mathematical operation to the corresponding utility method.
pfj-097.explanation: `Math.abs` returns an absolute value, `Math.sqrt` returns a square root, and `Math.pow` raises its first argument to the power of the second. These are static utility methods called on the Math class.

pfj-098.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-098.title: Calculating rectangle measurements
pfj-098.instructions: A Rectangle has width 8 and height 3. Which pair of results should its `getArea()` and `getPerimeter()` methods return?
hints: Area multiplies the two dimensions; perimeter adds all four sides.
pfj-098.explanation: The area is 8 × 3 = 24. The perimeter is 2 × (8 + 3) = 22.

pfj-099.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-099.title: Separating a local variable from an attribute
pfj-099.instructions:
A class has the following field:
```java
private int number = 42;
```
Its method declares this local variable:
```java
int number = 7;
```
The method then prints `number` followed by `this.number`. What is printed?
hints: An unqualified name resolves to the local variable when one shadows the field; `this` explicitly selects the current object’s attribute.
pfj-099.explanation: Inside the method, `number` refers to the local variable initialized to 7. `this.number` refers to the object attribute initialized to 42.

pfj-100.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-100.title: Understanding the effect of pass by value
pfj-100.instructions: A method receives an `int` parameter and increments that parameter. The caller passes its own variable `count`. After the method returns, what happens to the caller’s variable?
options: It keeps its original value because the method received a copy of the primitive value
It is always incremented because the parameter shares the variable
The call is invalid unless the method returns the parameter
hints: The method parameter is initialized with the argument value; it is a separate local variable.
pfj-100.explanation: The value of the primitive argument is copied into the method parameter. Incrementing the parameter changes only that local copy, not the caller’s variable.

pfj-101.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-101.title: Recognising compiled-language advantages
pfj-101.instructions: A team is evaluating a traditional compiled-language workflow. Which characteristics are advantages identified for that workflow in the course comparison? Select all that apply.
options: The compiler can perform checks before execution
The resulting binary can execute directly and quickly on its target processor
The source code can be reused across architectures, although separate target binaries are needed
The source code is not normally readable from the distributed binary
The same compiled binary is automatically suitable for every processor architecture
hints: Separate the benefits of compiling in advance from the limitation that the generated binary is target-specific.
pfj-101.explanation: The course lists compile-time checks, fast direct execution and source code that is not readable on the target as advantages. Source code is portable, but the compiled binary is platform-dependent; the original source is not interpreted on every run.

pfj-102.category: Programming Languages and the Java Platform
pfj-102.title: Recognising interpreted-language trade-offs
pfj-102.instructions: A team distributes a Python script to different operating systems. Which statements describe the interpreted-language model presented in the course? Select all that apply.
options: The source can be portable across platforms
A compatible interpreter must be available on each target system
The source is transformed during execution rather than compiled once into a target-specific executable beforehand
This approach can be slower because the transformation is needed during execution
The model guarantees compile-time checks before the program runs
The source is normally hidden from people using the target system
hints: Think about what must be installed on the target and when the source-to-execution transformation takes place.
pfj-102.explanation: Interpreted source is portable when a suitable interpreter is installed. The interpreter is needed on each target and translation occurs during execution. The course lists the lack of compile-time checks and readable source as disadvantages.

pfj-103.category: The Java Platform and Your First Java Program
pfj-103.title: Separating the roles of an IDE and a runtime
pfj-103.instructions: A user only needs to run an already compiled Java application. The computer has a suitable Java runtime installed but no development environment. Which statement is correct?
options: The application can run without an IDE; an IDE is a developer workbench, not the Java runtime
The application cannot run unless IntelliJ is installed
The IDE replaces the JVM when executing bytecode
The JDK compiler must be started manually for every run
hints: Distinguish tools that help a developer write and debug code from components required to execute bytecode.
pfj-103.explanation: An IDE assists development, but it is not required to run a compiled Java program. The runtime (including the JVM and Java API) is what the target needs to execute bytecode.

pfj-104.title: Recognising safe and explicit numeric conversions
pfj-104.instructions: Which statements about the following Java conversions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An `int` value can be assigned to a `double` without an explicit cast
A `double` value cannot normally be assigned to an `int` without an explicit cast
Casting a positive `double` to `int` discards its fractional part
Assigning an `int` to a `double` always loses the integer part
Integer division automatically preserves a fractional result when assigned to a `double`
hints: Consider whether the destination can represent the source value without narrowing and when the division itself is evaluated.
pfj-104.explanation: Converting an `int` to `double` is a widening conversion. Converting a `double` to `int` is narrowing and requires an explicit cast; the cast discards the fractional part. The type of the operands determines whether division is integer or floating-point.

pfj-105.title: Recognising equivalent range conditions
pfj-105.instructions: Which expressions both test whether `age` is between 18 and 67 inclusive? Select all that apply.
hints: One expression can state that both limits hold; another can state that neither invalid condition holds.
pfj-105.explanation: The first expression checks both inclusive bounds. The second negates the cases outside the range, making it logically equivalent. The OR condition is true for almost every age, and the strict comparisons exclude 18 and 67.

pfj-106.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-106.title: Using String methods to validate a code
options: The expression does not compile because `charAt` returns a String
hints: Evaluate the length check and the first-character check separately, then combine them with AND.
pfj-106.explanation: The String contains three characters, so `length() == 3` is true. Its character at index 0 is `A`, so the second comparison is also true. Both conditions hold, making `valid` true.

pfj-107.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-107.title: Distinguishing String and StringBuilder behavior
pfj-107.instructions: Which statements correctly describe the behavior of `String` and `StringBuilder` in Java? Select all that apply.
options: A String cannot be changed in place after it is created
Calling `concat` on a String returns a String result rather than changing the original object
Appending to a StringBuilder changes the builder’s contents
StringBuilder is useful when text is modified repeatedly
A StringBuilder append operation always creates a new builder object
hints: Compare whether each class is mutable and what happens to the object when text is appended or concatenated.
pfj-107.explanation: String is immutable, so operations such as `concat` return a new String. StringBuilder is mutable; append changes its existing contents and is more efficient for repeated modifications. Appending does not create a new builder each time.

pfj-108.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-108.title: Matching format specifiers to data
pfj-108.instructions: A report must display an integer count, a decimal amount, a name, a single character and a boolean status. Which format-specifier mapping is correct?
hints: Match each conversion with the Java value type it is intended to format.
pfj-108.explanation: `%d` formats integer values, `%f` floating-point values, `%s` Strings, `%c` characters and `%b` booleans. Each specifier must have a corresponding argument of a compatible type.

pfj-109.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-109.title: Choosing package-level access
pfj-109.instructions: A field must be accessible to classes in the same package but not directly accessible to unrelated classes in other packages. Which declaration provides that access level?
options: Declare the field with no accessibility modifier (package access)
hints: Compare package access with private, protected and public access.
pfj-109.explanation: Omitting an access modifier gives package access: classes in the same package can access the field, while unrelated classes in other packages cannot. Private is narrower; protected and public provide broader access.

pfj-110.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-110.title: Matching a public class to its source file
pfj-110.instructions:
A source file is named `Shape.java`, but its public top-level class is declared as follows:
```java
public class Rectangle
```
What must be corrected for the code to follow the Java file-naming rule taught in the course?
options: Rename the class to `ShapeApp` regardless of the file name
Move the class declaration into the main method
hints: The file name and the public top-level class name must match, including capitalization.
pfj-110.explanation: A public top-level class must be declared in a source file with the same name. Renaming the file to `Rectangle.java` brings the file and class declaration into sync.

pfj-111.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-111.title: Printing a percent sign with a format string
pfj-111.instructions: A report must contain the text `21% VAT`. Which formatting call correctly uses a value for the number and prints a literal percent sign?
hints: In a format string, percent introduces a conversion specifier; a literal percent sign needs its own escape form.
pfj-111.explanation: `%d` formats the integer 21. `%%` produces a literal percent character, so the output is `21% VAT`.

pfj-112.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-112.title: Using Math constants and comparison methods
pfj-112.instructions: A calculation needs the Java value of pi and must choose the larger of two measurements. Which expression uses the Math class appropriately?
hints: The course presents PI as a constant and max as a static method of the Math utility class.
pfj-112.explanation: `Math.PI` accesses the static constant, and `Math.max(first, second)` returns the larger of the two values. Static members are called using the class name rather than creating a Math object.

pfj-113.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-113.title: Simulating a coin toss
pfj-113.instructions: A program must simulate a fair coin toss and store the result as a boolean. Which code can directly produce `true` or `false` with equal probability?
hints: Choose the Random method whose result type is boolean.
pfj-113.explanation: `nextBoolean()` returns either true or false. `nextDouble()` returns a number in the interval from 0 inclusive to 1 exclusive, while the integer expressions shown do not produce a two-outcome range.

pfj-114.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-114.title: Generating a probability value
pfj-114.instructions: A simulation needs a random decimal value that is at least 0.0 but always less than 1.0. Which Random method directly returns a value in that interval?
hints: Consider which method returns a floating-point value rather than an integer or boolean.
pfj-114.explanation: `nextDouble()` returns a double in the interval 0 inclusive to 1 exclusive. The integer methods return whole numbers, and `nextBoolean()` returns a logical value.

pfj-115.category: Objects, References, Random, Strings and Formatting
pfj-115.title: Handling case-insensitive user input
pfj-115.instructions: A program should accept either `yes`, `YES` or `Yes` as confirmation. The user’s input is stored in a String named `answer`. Which test directly handles these casing variations?
hints: The comparison should check the complete text while deliberately ignoring uppercase/lowercase differences.
pfj-115.explanation: `equalsIgnoreCase` compares the String contents without considering casing. Comparing with `==` tests reference identity, while checking only the first character or length is not sufficient.

pfj-116.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-116.title: Predicting default values for several attributes
hints: Instance attributes receive defaults based on their declared types; a reference is not automatically an empty object.
pfj-116.explanation: A floating-point attribute defaults to 0.0, a boolean attribute to false, and an object-reference attribute such as String to null.

pfj-117.category: Classes, Attributes, Methods, Constructors and Math
pfj-117.title: Using Math.min for a lower bound
pfj-117.instructions: A program must select the smaller of two measurements without writing an `if` statement. Which call does that directly?
hints: Use the Math method whose purpose is to return the minimum of two values.
pfj-117.explanation: `Math.min(a, b)` returns the smaller argument. `Math.max` returns the larger, while `abs` and `sqrt` perform different operations.
